meta.title: ARCHÆOLOGY OF RUSSIAN DEATH
meta.subtitle: An Atlas of Death, Memory, Ritual and the Afterlife in Russian Culture
meta.editorial_note: All visible text is in English. Russian terms are given in simplified transliteration with a gloss. Quotations from Russian sources are the atlas’s working translations unless the source itself is in English. Dates before 1918 are given as they appear in the cited source; where a source converts to the New Style, the conversion is noted.

plates.title: THE THRESHOLD
plates.subtitle: The room, the moment, and the border that is not drawn
plates.dek: The ethnography of death in Russia is rarely an account of dying. It is an account of what the living do in the room afterwards — and of how quickly that room becomes a border.
plates.marginal: The mirror, the clock and the open window are the three objects most often repeated in the literature and the least often dated. None of them appears in a source earlier than the nineteenth century in the material used here.
plates.tradition: Orthodox Christian practice; local folk custom

sections.heading: A room with the window open
paras: In the accounts collected by ethnographers in Russian villages from the middle of the nineteenth century onward, death is registered less as an event than as a series of adjustments to a house. A window is opened. A mirror is covered. A clock is stopped. Water standing in a vessel is covered or carried out. The body is washed and laid on a bench or table, head toward the icons, and the household is rearranged around it.

These are the practices most often repeated in the literature, and they are the ones most often flattened into a single ‘Russian custom’. The sources do not support that flattening. They record variants; they record disagreement between villages a day’s walk apart; and they record the informant’s own uncertainty about why a thing was done.

sections.alt: A log house with carved window frames and a rusted iron roof, its windows empty, tall grass in front
sections.caption: An abandoned izba with carved window frames, Nepogodikha, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast. Photograph: Evgeny Katyshev, CC BY-SA 3.0. The house is the first boundary in the material this plate uses: what is done at its windows, doors and threshold is done for the person who is leaving it.
sections.credit: Evgeny Katyshev / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

sections.heading: The soul as breath, and as a guest
paras: Russian folk belief, as described by Linda Ivanits and by D. K. Zelenin before her, treats the soul (*dusha*) as a substance closely bound to breath and to the body’s warmth, and simultaneously as a person-like visitor who must be housed, fed and escorted. These are not two beliefs held by different people; they are two grammars used in the same account.

The consequence is a threshold that is both physical and social. The dead remain members of the household for a defined period, are addressed in the second person, and are given food and a place at the table. The border is maintained by small prohibitions rather than by a wall.

sections.heading: Premonitions, and the problem of the motif
paras: A dog howling at night, a bird striking the window, a beam groaning in the wall, a double shadow: the folkloric record is full of signs read retrospectively as announcements of a death. Published collections treat them as motifs, not as statistics. No source used here establishes how widely any single sign was believed, and retrospective reading makes such reports structurally unreliable.

sections.heading: Three claims we did not confirm
items: That the mirror was covered to prevent the soul from being trapped. The practice is widely reported; the explanation is supplied by later writers and varies.
That a body was always carried out feet first. Reported in some regional descriptions; we did not verify its distribution or age.

That the forty-day period is pre-Christian in origin. The scheme is documented in Orthodox liturgical handbooks; the claim that it continues an older pagan calendar is an interpretation, and a contested one.

sections.text: The dead person is not yet an ancestor. For forty days he is a guest who has not been given a room.
sections.attrib: Editorial note, not a quotation from a source

plates.title: THE BODY
plates.subtitle: Washing, dressing, carrying
plates.dek: Before it becomes a memory, the dead is an object that must be handled. The handling is the ritual.

sections.heading: Washing
paras: The body is washed (*obmyvanie*) before it is dressed. The task is generally given to people from outside the immediate family — commonly older women, sometimes women who have performed it before — and the work is understood as a service that must be paid for, in soap, towels or money. The washing is practical and it is also a boundary: the living handle the dead at arm’s length and then wash themselves.

The water used is not poured out where the household draws water. In accounts from different provinces it is carried away, poured at a threshold, or given to the ground. The variation is the point: the sources describe a prohibition around disposal, not one fixed method.

sections.alt: Mourners stand around an open grave among cut branches, a plain wooden coffin on the ground beside them
sections.caption: A burial photographed c. 1941–43 by a German soldier. The Bundesarchiv caption says the body was taken out of the coffin and committed to the earth in a blanket; the coffin stays above ground. Bundesarchiv, Bild 169-0339, CC BY-SA 3.0 de. The place is uncertain: Commons files the picture under both Russia and Ukraine.

sections.heading: Clothing kept for the occasion
paras: Dress for the dead was, in many households, prepared during life and stored: a bundle known in different places as *smertnoe* — ‘the death clothes’. It might include linen, a shirt or dress, stockings, sometimes a shroud. To have it ready was considered a form of decency, and its absence a small scandal.

Once dressed, the body was placed in the coffin and the coffin placed so that the dead faced the icons. The position is an argument in wood and cloth: the dead is oriented toward the images of salvation, not toward the household. The living keep the door; the dead keep the corner.

sections.heading: The coffin as furniture

meta.Material: Planks; surviving dugout examples in northern descriptions

paras: The coffin (*grob*) appears in the ethnography with an emphasis on plainness, but also with ornament: a lid, a shawl, a cross on the lid. In some northern descriptions coffins were hollowed from a single trunk; by the late imperial period the sawn plank coffin was standard and increasingly a purchased object rather than a made one.
Between the two lies a commercial history that the ritual sources rarely discuss: the coffin is where the funeral economy becomes visible, first as carpentry, later as an industry.

sections.heading: Why the body is a difficult archive
items: The body leaves no object. What survives is the description of the objects that surrounded it, written down later, often by outsiders.
Ethnographers of the nineteenth century tended to record what they judged to be old. The date of a practice is therefore often the date of its recording, not of its origin.

plates.title: THE RITUAL
plates.subtitle: Days three, nine, forty
plates.dek: The most confidently repeated ‘Russian funeral custom’ is also the one most often misdescribed: the commemoration on the third, ninth and fortieth day is a liturgical scheme before it is a folk one.
plates.marginal: The third, ninth and fortieth days are often introduced as an ancient Slavic custom. The handbook quoted on this plate is a Christian explanation of a Christian cycle; the older layer, if it exists, has not been demonstrated here.
plates.period: Liturgical sources 17th–19th c.; practice recorded 19th–21st c.

sections.heading: The shape of the forty days
paras: The commemoration of the dead on the third, ninth and fortieth day after death is set out in Orthodox liturgical handbooks, and the reasons given there are theological rather than calendrical. In the nineteenth-century handbook *Novaia Skrizhal’*, the third day is tied to the Resurrection, the ninth to the nine ranks of angels, and the fortieth to the Ascension, which took place on the fortieth day.

The same handbook is explicit that the prayers are for the forgiveness of sins and the placing of the soul ‘with the saints’. The popular explanations that accompany the scheme — that the soul visits the house for three days, that it is examined on the ninth, that it finally departs on the fortieth — belong to a different register. They are widespread, they are recorded, and they are not the doctrine.

sections.alt: A coloured print of a staircase rising through clouds, with demons and angels on the steps and a deathbed at the lower left
sections.caption: *Death of Theodora*: a Russian hand-made lubok, second half of the 19th century, showing the soul’s ascent past the aerial toll-houses (*mytarstva*). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. The forty days are also an itinerary in popular print; this is an image from print culture, not a record of what a village did.
sections.credit: Anonymous lubok / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

sections.heading: Against the survival story
paras: Nineteenth- and early twentieth-century scholarship often read Russian funerary practice as a survival of pre-Christian religion, with the Church imposed on top. Later work on ritual has been more cautious. A. K. Baiburin’s study of ritual in traditional culture treats ritual as a system of signs with its own internal logic rather than as a fossil of an earlier belief; the question of what a rite ‘originally meant’ is usually unanswerable from the evidence that survives.

This atlas therefore marks origin claims as interpretations. The forty-day cycle is documented as Christian. Whether some households also understood it as an older calendar is a question the sources used here cannot settle.

sections.heading: Who does the work
paras: The ritual has an economy of roles. The priest serves; a reader may read the psalter; women lament; neighbours cook and carry. The laments (see plate G) are performed by women who are often, but not always, kin, and their performance is judged — for voice, for fullness, for the ability to make the room weep.
The distribution of labour is itself historical. In the Soviet period the priest’s role contracted and the household’s expanded; after 1991 it contracted back again in some places and not in others.

sections.heading: One calendar, many calendars
items: The dates of commemoration interact with the church calendar (and with the Julian calendar still used by part of the Russian Church). A date given in a source may not correspond to the date a family used.
Memorial days also differ by region and by parish practice. The scheme above is a frame, not a census.

plates.title: THE TABLE
plates.subtitle: Feeding the dead, feeding the living
plates.dek: The memorial meal is the place where the dead is most directly treated as a person with preferences, a place and an appetite.

sections.heading: The hot dinner
paras: On the day of burial the household feeds everyone who came. In the ethnography this meal has a name in each region — ‘hot dinner’, ‘hot table’ — and a fixed grammar: a first course that is eaten before anything else, a place kept for the dead, a portion set aside, food carried to the grave.

The meal is commemoration, and it is also accounting: those who washed, dug, carried, read and cooked are fed, and the household’s obligation is discharged in food. To refuse to sit at the table is to refuse the account.

sections.heading: Kutia, and the ambiguity of grain
paras: Kutya is boiled grain sweetened with honey, and in its church form — *kolivo* — it is brought to the memorial service and blessed. The grain is read as a figure of resurrection: it is buried, it does not remain buried. The reading is old and it is also obvious enough to have been made many times independently.

What the sources do not settle is the relationship between the church dish and the household dish. In some accounts they are the same object under two names; in others the household kutya is a separate, richer preparation with raisins or nuts. The atlas keeps both, and keeps the question open.

sections.alt: People standing among graves in a cemetery, with food and cloths laid on the graves
sections.caption: Commemoration at graves, Khutir Tymky, Ukraine, 2014. Photograph: Perohanych, CC BY-SA 3.0. Included as a documented example outside the Russian Federation — not as evidence for Russian practice.

sections.heading: Why a Ukrainian photograph is here
items: The atlas treats ‘Russian’ as a language, a state tradition and a set of institutions, not as a synonym for East Slavic. Where a photograph documents a Ukrainian or Belarusian practice, it is labelled as such.
The meal at the grave is widely attested across the region, which makes it exactly the kind of practice that gets mislabelled as ‘Russian’ by default.

sections.alt: A nineteenth-century photograph of people seated at a table outdoors at a cemetery
sections.caption: The same 1881 photograph at its archive resolution, before processing. The atlas shows the degraded copy at the head of this plate because that is how the image would have circulated.

plates.title: THE RETURNING DEAD
plates.subtitle: The unclean dead and the trouble with categories
plates.dek: Not every dead person was thought to stay dead. The distinction was not good and evil but proper and improper death — and the category that names it has been under dispute for a century.

sections.heading: Zelenin’s ‘pledged’ dead
paras: In 1916 D. K. Zelenin published a study of those who die an unnatural death — by suicide, accident, murder, drowning, or before their time — and of the rusalki. His term for them, *zalozhnye pokoiniki*, is usually translated as ‘pledged’ or ‘unclean’ dead: those whose death was not completed within the order of things.

Zelenin argued that such dead were buried apart, outside the cemetery or at its edge, in ravines, fields or at crossroads, and that they were believed to remain active — to walk, to appear, to harm. The book is a work of synthesis and it is also a work of its time, assembled from scattered reports into a system that no single informant would have recognised.

sections.heading: The dispute
paras: Later scholarship has treated Zelenin’s category with caution. The reports he gathered come from different provinces, different decades and different genres — legend, memorate, custom, ecclesiastical prohibition — and the boundary between ‘unclean’ and ‘clean’ death was drawn differently from place to place. Whether the rusalka is a development of the unclean dead, as Zelenin proposed, remains an interpretation rather than a finding.
The atlas therefore presents *zalozhnye* as a scholarly construction built on real reports, not as a folk taxonomy that everyone shared. The reports are evidence. The category is an argument.

sections.heading: Case notes, without the case

meta.Warning: No individual narrative is quoted here

paras: The reports share a structure: a death that violates expectation, a burial that violates place, and a subsequent sighting or disturbance. The disturbance is usually resolved by a ritual action — moving the body, reading a prayer, driving a stake, calling the priest — and the resolution tells us more about the living than about the dead.

No narrative is reproduced verbatim in this atlas. The genre is highly variable, the published texts are often retold rather than transcribed, and a single vivid quotation would misrepresent the record as more uniform than it is.

sections.heading: What the category was for
paras: The unclean dead mark the limits of the community’s obligation. They are the people for whom the full ritual was not, or could not be, performed — and the fear they provoke is the fear of an obligation left unpaid. In this reading the revenant is less a monster than an unpaid debt with a voice.
That reading is the atlas’s interpretation, offered as such. It does not require the dead to be real; it requires the living to have accounts.

sections.heading: No vampires here
items: Russian and Ukrainian records do contain stories of the dead who rise and feed, and the word *upyr’* is attested. It is not the same figure as the nineteenth-century literary vampire, and it should not be used to give this material a familiar costume.
The atlas avoids the vocabulary of horror. ‘Returning’ is a social event in these sources, not a genre.

sections.text: A bad death is the one that leaves something owing, not the one that hurts most.

plates.title: THE GRAVE
plates.subtitle: From churchyard to cemetery, and the architecture of a name
plates.dek: The Russian grave is a legal object before it is a sacred one. Where the dead may lie has been decided by decrees, epidemics and municipal budgets at least as often as by custom.
plates.location: Moscow, St Petersburg, Pushkin, provincial Russia

sections.heading: The decree of 1723
paras: By a decree of Peter I dated 10 October 1723, burials inside towns were restricted — ‘except for notable persons’ — because the churchyards at churches and monasteries had become overcrowded. The same decree ordered the levelling of raised tombs and the replacement of relief images on shrines with painted ones.

The measure did not last. After Peter’s death in 1725, churchyard burial resumed, and it took the catastrophe of 1771 to produce a durable change. In that year plague in Moscow killed in the tens of thousands, and the new cemetery at Vagankovo was founded to receive them; the first burials there were unnamed Muscovites.

sections.heading: The cemetery as a municipal object
paras: From the late eighteenth century the cemetery moved out of the parish and into the city’s administration: walls, gates, a plan, a register, a fee. The dead acquired an address. This is the moment at which the Russian cemetery becomes legible as an institution — and the moment at which the difference between a churchyard and a necropolis becomes visible.

By the nineteenth century the cemetery was also a place of class. The monastery necropolis, the merchant plot, the communal trench and the unconsecrated ground outside the wall were all parts of one landscape, and they were not equally maintained.

sections.alt: A 1913 halftone illustration showing stone tombs and monuments crowded together in a monastery necropolis
sections.caption: The Georgian necropolis at Donskoy Monastery, Moscow. Illustration from *Letopis’ Gruzii*, edited by B. Esadze, 1913. Public domain; duotone processing by the atlas.
sections.credit: Public domain; derivative processing by the atlas

sections.alt: A wooden cross with a small gabled roof, standing in a snowy cemetery among other crosses
sections.caption: A roofed cross (*golubets*) at Kazan cemetery, Pushkin, near St Petersburg. Photograph: CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons. The type is often described as northern; this example is from the outskirts of the imperial capital.

sections.heading: The roof over the cross
paras: The *golubets* — a cross sheltered by a small gabled roof, sometimes enclosed as a little house — is one of the most distinctive grave forms recorded in the Russian North and in old cemeteries elsewhere. The roof protects the wood; it also makes the cross into a building, and the grave into a dwelling.
The atlas does not map its distribution. Published claims about the ‘northern’ range of the form rest on surveys this project has not consulted, and a photograph of one example is not a distribution.

sections.alt: Schematic plan of a walled cemetery with rows of graves, a chapel, a gate and a red route line
sections.caption: Schematic cemetery plan: wall, gate, chapel, rows of graves, and the route taken by a funeral. Drawn for this atlas; not a survey of any existing cemetery.

sections.alt: Crosses of different shapes standing in deep snow among bare trees in a city cemetery
sections.caption: Crosses of several shapes in one field, Zaretskoe Cemetery, Petrozavodsk, January 2019. Photograph: Semenov.m7, CC0. The type of a cross is read off the monuments themselves: one shape for the plot, another for the next.

sections.heading: Novodevichy: the necropolis as biography
paras: Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow became, in the Soviet period, the place where the state buried its recognised dead: writers, scientists, generals, cosmonauts. The graves are biographical objects. The stonecutter’s lettering, the portrait, the open book, the ship, the aircraft — each monument is a curriculum vitae in granite.

Two examples recorded in the photographs used by this atlas: the grave of Ilya Ilf, and a double monument for the writer A. N. Stepanov and his wife, designed — according to the photographer’s description — as two ships on a dark sea. The atlas repeats that description as a description, not as a documented intention of the family.

sections.heading: Portraits on stone
items: Photographic portraits set into headstones are a familiar feature of late-Soviet and post-Soviet cemeteries. The atlas has not found a scholarly source for their chronology and does not date them here.
The same caution applies to the enamel photograph, the plastic wreath and the metal fence: visible everywhere, documented in the sources used here almost nowhere.

sections.alt: A carved stone monument on the grave of Ilya Ilf at Novodevichy Cemetery
sections.caption: The grave of Ilya Ilf, Novodevichy Cemetery, Moscow. Photograph: Ghirlandajo, CC BY 3.0. The monument is biographical: the lettering, the stone and the plot are all part of the state necropolis.

sections.alt: A grave monument carved as two ships at Novodevichy Cemetery
sections.caption: The grave of A. N. Stepanov and M. A. Stepanova, Novodevichy. The monument is carved as two ships; the photographer records the family’s plan as the source of the design, and the atlas repeats that as a description, not as a documented intention.

plates.title: THE VOICE
plates.subtitle: Lament, euphemism, and the grammar of address
plates.dek: The dead are spoken to. The grammar of that address is one of the most precisely recorded things in Russian ethnography — and one of the least often quoted accurately.
plates.location: Olonets province (Karelia) and the Russian North

sections.heading: Barsov’s north
paras: Between 1872 and 1886 E. V. Barsov published *Prichitaniia Severnogo kraia* — ‘Laments of the Northern Land’ — in three volumes. The collection is the foundational document of Russian lament studies: texts recorded in the Olonets region, with the circumstances of performance, the performers and their repertoires.

Laments are not spontaneous weeping set to words; they are composed in performance from a stock of formulas, by performers who know the genre and are judged by it. Barsov’s volumes make this visible: the same formulas recur across different deaths, recombined.

sections.alt: Arc diagram with three stations
sections.caption: Placeholder schematic retained for the plate sequence.

sections.heading: The score of a lament

meta.Form: Formulaic, performed, address in the second person

paras: An analytical reconstruction of the genre’s movement, after Barsov’s volumes: an address to the dead; a question about the journey; a complaint against the household’s new order; self-reproach by the survivor; a description of the grave; a farewell that refuses to be final. The order is not fixed, and the performer may return to any station.

This is a structural description, not a text. The atlas does not print a lament here because a responsible quotation requires collation against a printed source and a translation the reader can check, and this edition has done neither.

sections.heading: The second person
paras: Russian funerary language keeps the dead in the second person and in the present tense for as long as the ritual lasts. The dead is addressed by kin term — ‘my child’, ‘my master’, ‘my sister’ — and asked questions that presume an answer. The euphemisms that surround death in ordinary speech (*ushel* — ‘he has gone’; *ne stalo* — ‘he is no more’) are suspended in the lament, where the dead is named and spoken to directly.
Death is not denied here. The border is held by hand: the dead person counts as present for exactly as long as the ritual lasts, and is then let go.

sections.heading: What is not quoted
items: No laments, proverbs or epitaphs are reproduced verbatim in this edition. Every one of them would require a check against a printed text and a defensible translation.
The atlas prefers an honest silence to a decorative quotation. Where a phrase appears in quotation marks, it is either from a source listed in the bibliography or explicitly marked as editorial.

sections.attrib: Bibliographic title: E. V. Barsov, Laments of the Northern Land, Moscow, 1872–1886. Russian title, not a quotation from the laments.

plates.title: THE AFTERLIFE
plates.subtitle: Doctrine, image, and the soul’s itinerary
plates.dek: Orthodox teaching about the dead is precise, and it is not the same thing as the crowded cosmology of the icon. The atlas keeps the two apart, then puts them on the same page.
plates.period: Iconography 15th–18th c.; doctrine and practice to the present

sections.heading: What the Church says
paras: Orthodox teaching holds that the dead are judged and that the living may pray for them. The funeral rites ask for the forgiveness of sins and for a place ‘with the saints’; memorial services repeat the request at intervals. The fortieth day is the last of the appointed commemorations; the annual commemoration continues after it.

The Church’s language is deliberately restrained about the intermediate state. Where popular literature supplies a detailed itinerary — where the soul goes on which day, what it sees — the atlas marks that as devotional or folk elaboration, not as doctrine.

sections.alt: A large eighteenth-century Russian icon of the Last Judgment, densely painted with registers of saints, angels, scales, a river of fire and compartments of punishment
sections.caption: The Last Judgment. Volga region, 1770s–1780s. Tempera on wood, 180 × 137 cm. The icon is dense with inscribed texts and compartments; it is a picture that expects to be read.

sections.heading: Reading the icon
paras: The Last Judgment icon is a diagram as much as a painting. Christ appears in glory; the scales weigh souls; the righteous move toward the heavenly city; the damned descend into a river of fire; the punishments are arranged in small compartments, each with its own inscription and its own social type — the miser, the adulterer, the usurer, the drunkard.

The Volga icon used here belongs to the eighteenth century and to the urban artisan milieu: it borrows heavily from printed engravings, including their page-like blocks of text. This is no remote medieval image but a picture grown out of print, made for people used to reading with their eyes.

sections.alt: A fifteenth-century icon of the Dormition of the Mother of God, with the apostles gathered around a bed and Christ holding her soul
sections.caption: The Dormition of the Mother of God. Novgorod, from the Desyatinny Monastery; icon of the fifteenth century. The Dormition is the model of the good death: a death that is also a birth.

sections.heading: Theology is not a mood
items: The icon’s punishments are evidence of a moral taxonomy, so the atlas does not use them as atmosphere or decoration.
Where a popular belief contradicts or exceeds the Church’s formulation, the atlas says so rather than harmonising them.

plates.title: COLLECTIVE DEATH
plates.subtitle: Plague, war, and the state’s arithmetic of the dead
plates.dek: Mass death produces two things at once: a hole in the record and an official number. The atlas is interested in the gap between them.
plates.marginal: At Piskaryovskoye the count is given as about 470,000 in some accounts and about 520,000 in others. The gap is no rounding error: the two figures count different things.
plates.tradition: State commemoration; Orthodox and secular rites

sections.heading: 1771: the pit
paras: The Moscow plague of 1771 killed in the tens of thousands. The dead were buried outside the city, and the new cemetery at Vagankovo received, first of all, unnamed people. The historical account of the cemetery begins with a number it cannot disaggregate.
Mass death produces this kind of record: a pit, a total, a name for the place, no names for the people. The atlas does not illustrate the pit. It prints the fact of it.

sections.alt: A long row of low granite blocks with an eternal flame burning in front of a bronze sculpture
sections.caption: Piskaryovskoye Memorial Cemetery, St Petersburg. The memorial was opened on 9 May 1960; the flame was lit from the fire on the Field of Mars. The cemetery holds victims of the Leningrad blockade and soldiers of the Leningrad Front.

sections.heading: The unknown soldier
paras: The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Kremlin wall was opened on 8 May 1967. The monument was designed by the architects Dmitrii Burdin, Vladimir Klimov and Iurii Rabaev, with the sculptor Nikolai Tomskii; the remains had been brought from a mass grave outside Moscow. The eternal flame was lit at the opening and has been maintained since.

The unknown soldier is a very specific solution to a problem of scale: it converts an unmanageable number into a single body that can be visited. What it gains in ritual focus it loses in information. The state’s memory is built on that trade.

sections.alt: A black-and-white photograph of a crowd laying flowers at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, with honour guards
sections.caption: Laying flowers at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, 9 May 1979. Photograph: I. Burov, Glavarkhiv Moscow; CC BY 4.0.
sections.credit: I. Burov / Glavarkhiv Moscow, CC BY 4.0

sections.heading: Unburied
paras: Alexander Etkind’s *Warped Mourning* argues that Soviet culture was shaped by deaths that were not buried properly — the executed, the disappeared, the dead in unmarked ground — and that literature and memory-work in Russia have repeatedly returned to them as the ‘undead’. The argument is a cultural history, not a survey of graves, and the atlas presents it as an interpretation.

Catherine Merridale’s *Night of Stone* makes a related point from the side of the living: the twentieth century in Russia produced so much death that mourning itself became a skill that had to be managed, suppressed, or performed in private. Both books are used here for their arguments, not as inventories of fact.

sections.heading: Why there are no bodies here
items: This plate uses no photographs of corpses, no photographs of starving people, no images of the blockade dead. The atlas treats these as deaths, not as imagery.
The monuments are shown because they are what the state built, and because their surfaces are evidence of how memory was organised.

sections.alt: The Motherland Calls statue seen across the Mamayev Kurgan memorial complex
sections.caption: Mamayev Kurgan, Volgograd: the memorial complex on the site of the Stalingrad fighting. Photograph: Redboston, CC BY-SA 4.0.

plates.title: DEATH IN ART
plates.subtitle: The sled, the black square, and the deathbed as an argument
plates.dek: Russian art tends to approach death through a single object held at an angle: a coffin on a sled, a square on a wall, a body on a bed.

sections.heading: Perov, 1865
paras: Vasily Perov’s *Seeing Off the Dead* (*Provody pokoinika*, 1865; oil on canvas, 45.3 × 57 cm; Tretyakov Gallery, inv. 5248) is small, and it is composed around a box. A peasant family rides a sled through snow; the coffin is tied behind them; a dog runs alongside. The widow sits with her back to us; the children face us.
What the picture shows is a delivery. The body is hauled across a landscape that takes no notice: huge sky, flat snow, a few bare trees. Grief here behaves like weather.

The Tretyakov Gallery’s own catalogue note connects the painting to Nekrasov’s poem *Frost, Red Nose* (1862–63), which describes a peasant family that has lost its breadwinner. The comparison was made by contemporaries and has been repeated by art historians; it is a documented reception, not a proof of intention.

sections.alt: Painting: a peasant family in a horse-drawn sled carrying a wooden coffin across a snowy field under a vast grey sky
sections.caption: Vasily Perov, *Seeing Off the Dead*, 1865. Oil on canvas, 45.3 × 57 cm. Tretyakov Gallery, inv. 5248. Photographic reproduction: public domain.
sections.credit: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons; collection: Tretyakov Gallery

sections.heading: The deathbed as a room
paras: Russian prose of the nineteenth century returns again and again to the deathbed as a place where a life is suddenly legible. Tolstoy’s *The Death of Ivan Ilyich* (1886) is built as a corridor: the dying man moves through pain, denial and an unexpected opening at the end. Chekhov’s early story *The Death of a Clerk* (1883) makes the same subject ridiculous: a man dies of embarrassment. Bunin’s *The Gentleman from San Francisco* (1915) puts a wealthy man’s death in a hotel and refuses to grant it dignity.
Three stories, three verdicts, no common school. Each uses a death to test the social order, and each gets a different result.

sections.heading: The square that was a gravestone
paras: Kazimir Malevich died in 1935 and was buried, according to the account in the Moscow press, near Nemchinovka outside Moscow, under a lone oak. A white cube with a black square was placed on the grave. The oak was later cut down, the grave was lost, and the cube disappeared.

What survives is a photograph and a painting. The black square began as an argument about painting, turned into a grave marker, and then vanished. Nowhere else in this atlas does an artwork and a missing grave coincide so exactly.

sections.alt: The Perov painting reduced to a high-contrast halftone dot screen
sections.caption: The same painting, halftoned. The screen is a reproduction technology, not a style: it is how the image would have reached most viewers in print.
sections.credit: Derivative of a public-domain image; halftone processing by the atlas

sections.heading: On not illustrating grief
items: No literary quotations appear on this plate. Passages describing dying are easy to excerpt and hard to excerpt honestly.
The paintings are shown at their own proportions. Cropping is used once, deliberately, on the halftone detail.

plates.title: THE SOVIET AFTERLIFE
plates.subtitle: Cremation, the civil funeral, and the industry that followed
plates.dek: The Soviet state kept the funeral and rebuilt it as a ceremony of the collective; then the collective dissolved.
plates.tradition: State secular ritual; Orthodox revival; commercial funeral services

sections.heading: A crematorium in a church
paras: In 1925 the Moscow Soviet decided to build a crematorium and chose, as its site, the church of St Seraphim of Sarov and St Anna of Kashin at the Donskoy Monastery. The furnace was made by a German firm; the first cremation took place on 12 January 1927, and the official opening was held on 6 October 1927, without ceremony, according to the Moscow press account.
A church built for burying bodies and praying for the dead became a furnace for making them disappear. The state did not have to design a new building; it confiscated one.

sections.heading: The civil funeral
paras: The Soviet funeral was a ceremony without a priest: a hall, a portrait, an orchestra, a speech, a red coffin, medals carried on cushions, a grave in a designated section. The ritual was designed to be legible, repeatable and secular, and it was administered by the same municipal apparatus that handled housing and sanitation.

Grief did not go away. It got a script and a timetable. Merridale’s account of the twentieth century is largely about what happened when the script and the experience did not match — and about the private, domestic mourning that continued alongside the public one.

sections.caption: Dates and decisions, with sources
rows: Moscow Soviet decides to build a crematorium
Tomb of the Unknown Soldier opened
End of the state funeral monopoly; commercial services expand

sections.heading: After 1991
paras: The post-Soviet funeral is a market. Private funeral homes, municipal cemeteries with fee schedules, monument workshops, wreath sellers and, more recently, online memorial pages form an industry that the Soviet system had tried to keep inside the state. Orthodox practice returned in parallel — sometimes inside the same funeral, with the priest arriving after the orchestra.

The atlas has not found a reliable scholarly account of this transition in the sources used here. This section is therefore marked as an editorial sketch, and the digital memorial is marked as an open question rather than described as a fact.

sections.heading: The digital grave
items: Online memorial pages, QR codes on headstones and social-media profiles of the dead are visible in contemporary Russia, but the atlas has not verified their scale, chronology or legal status.
They are recorded here as a research task, not as a finding.

sections.text: The state could arrange the funeral. The mourning stayed with the families.
sections.attrib: Editorial note, after Merridale and Etkind

sections.alt: A black cast-iron cross with an oval enamel portrait, plastic flowers in front, black granite stelae among pines
sections.caption: Besovets Cemetery, Petrozavodsk, October 2022. Photograph: Mikhail Semyonov, CC BY-SA 4.0. A cast cross with an enamel portrait, plastic flowers, and black granite stelae behind: the vocabulary of the post-Soviet plot, in one town’s cemetery. It stands for no scale or trend.
sections.credit: Mikhail Semyonov / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

plates.title: THE UNFINISHED ARCHIVE
plates.subtitle: What is missing, and how to draw it
plates.dek: This plate is mostly empty on purpose: an atlas of death that showed everything would be lying about the record.
plates.marginal: A register that lists what is missing is still a register. The empty column is the most honest part of this plate.
plates.tradition: Archive, ruin, and the digital trace

sections.heading: The record has holes
paras: Cemeteries are destroyed for reasons that are rarely stated as destruction: a road, a park, a housing block, a sports facility. The dead are moved, or not moved; the stones are reused as paving or foundation; the register is lost. What remains is a place-name and a photograph taken before.

This plate collects the forms of absence the atlas has actually encountered: a grave whose monument has disappeared, a cemetery photographed but not surveyed, a photograph whose subject is unidentified, a practice described only in a footnote.

sections.alt: A weathered stone tomb with a broken cross and overgrown grass in an abandoned cemetery
sections.caption: Abandoned tomb, Nizhne-Gnilovskoye cemetery, Rostov-on-Don. Photograph released CC0. The tomb is not a monument to anyone in particular; it is a monument to maintenance.

sections.heading: Register of losses
rows: lost; the cube disappeared, the oak was cut down
partly destroyed in the Soviet period
maintained by memory, not by record
Names of the 1771 plague dead at Vagankovo

sections.heading: How to draw a hole
paras: The atlas uses three devices for absence: a blank field with a single line of type; a photograph printed too faintly to read; a register in which the status column says ‘lost’ and the evidence column says nothing.
None of these reconstructs anything. They show where the research stops, and this is the one place in the atlas where a page may stay almost empty.

sections.heading: What would be needed
items: A field survey of at least one provincial cemetery, with photographs, dates and a condition record.
Access to a municipal burial register, even a fragmentary one.
A scholarly source on post-Soviet digital memorials.
The atlas is published with these gaps visible rather than filled.

sections.text: The archive keeps losing pages, and the loss is part of how it is made.

sections.alt: A dark wooden house with a sagging roof beside a country road under a pale sky
sections.caption: An abandoned wooden house by the road, Tver Oblast, August 2016. Photograph: Rakoon, CC0. The empty house is a second kind of cemetery record: nobody keeps it, and nobody has said it is gone.

plates.title: THE EMPTY HOUSE
plates.subtitle: What the rite does to a house, and what the census says about empty ones
plates.dek: In the Eastern Slavic funeral material the house takes part in a death: its windows are opened, its boundaries are said to break. Decades later the state counts villages with no one in them. The two bodies of evidence are different, and this plate keeps them apart.
plates.marginal: The ritual sources describe houses in which someone has died. The census counts villages in which no one lives. Nothing in the sources used here links the two, so the plate does not.
plates.location: Eastern Slavic traditions (corpus partly outside Russia); Russian Federation (census)
plates.tradition: Eastern Slavic folk custom and Orthodox practice

sections.heading: A house that has been broken
paras: Maria Andryunina’s survey of Ukrainian, Belarusian, western Russian and Polish funeral rites reports that at a death doors and windows were opened and holes made in the roof or ceiling, so that death could come in and the soul go out. By her account the house was then treated as broken. Its sacred boundaries were annulled, and an unsettled soul could haunt it, which made it dangerous for the living.

The corpus matters. The rites in that article come from the western and southern fringes of the Eastern Slavic world and from Poland, and the plate does not offer them as a single Russian custom. The same article reports the reverse for new buildings: a newly built house counted as incomplete until the first death within it.

sections.alt: The red corner of a wooden izba: icons on a shelf, an embroidered towel and a bench along the log wall
sections.caption: The red corner of an izba at Vitoslavlitsy, Veliky Novgorod: icons, a towel, a bench. A museum interior, not the record of any family’s room. Photograph: Aglav, CC BY-SA 3.0.

sections.heading: The window
paras: Jelena Lewkijewskaja’s study of the window in the traditional culture of the Eastern Slavs treats it as a ritual entrance and exit between this world and the other. In funeral rites and in legends about death it is the route by which the souls of the dead, and mythological figures, enter and leave the house. Throwing something out of a window is a way of disposing of a dangerous or impure thing. In the same tradition a house without windows is the dwelling of someone alien, a being from another world.

Put beside the open windows of the deathbed, this gives a dwelling whose openings are working parts of the rite. The study is five pages long and generalises across all the Eastern Slavs, and only its abstract was available to the atlas. It frames the question; it does not describe any one village.

sections.heading: The coffin as a house
paras: Anna Plotnikova’s essay on the earthly places of death starts from the Slavic idea of death as a passage to another world, where the dead acquire a home. The coffin, the grave and the graveyard are read as that home’s earthly forms. A coffin is sometimes built like a house, with window openings, and its inside can copy a living home: an icon corner, bedding, everyday things. Funeral laments call it a cold, dark house without windows, and some words for ‘coffin’ derive from the word for ‘house’.

On the same reading the dead remain tied to the home they left, and funeral customs work at separating them from it, by changing the route out of the house or by removing the dead person’s belongings. The essay covers Slavic traditions broadly. Which of these details are recorded for Russian regions has not yet been traced, and the bibliographic record for the essay is incomplete (see the source note).

sections.heading: Counting the empty village
rows: TASS, 16 Dec 2011, on the official 2010 census report
19,400 villages without inhabitants, 48% more than at the previous census
Villages that exist de jure with no registered residents
134,000 villages in total, 8,500 fewer than in 2002
RTE, 6 Apr 2011, citing the head of Rosstat
Uninhabited villages up from 13,000 to 19,400; 36,200 villages with fewer than ten residents

sections.heading: What an uninhabited village is, and is not
items: A village counted as uninhabited has no registered residents at the census. The figure does not say whether its houses still stand, who owns them or whether anyone returns in summer. The three reports count three different things, and the atlas does not turn them into a number of empty houses. The Rosstat tables were not consulted, only reports of them.

None of the sources used here records beliefs about abandoned houses in Russian regions. The ritual material on this plate concerns houses in which someone has died, not houses that were left. Whether the two connect is a research lead, not a finding.

sections.alt: A dark wooden house with a sagging roof beside a country road under a pale sky
sections.caption: A wooden house beside a road, Tver Oblast, August 2016. Photograph: Rakoon, CC0. The photograph shows a house; it cannot show why the house is empty.

sections.heading: What would turn this plate into a study
items: Regional ethnographic records of what was done with a house after a death, with village, year and collector named.
Household inventories and probate records for rural homes, where archives allow access.
Oral-history collections on leaving a village house, with consent and attribution settled for any private testimony.
The Rosstat census tables themselves, with the definition of an uninhabited settlement.

plates.title: THE FOREST EDGE
plates.subtitle: Burial away from the churchyard, the forest on the road to the dead, and a hut at the border
plates.dek: Three kinds of evidence put the dead near the forest: reports of burial in forest ravines, a belief that the way to the dead leads through the woods, and a fairy-tale hut at the treeline. They come from different peoples and different genres, and the plate does not blend them.
plates.marginal: One report is about Mordvins. One article is mostly Estonian and Belarusian. One is a reading of folktales. None of them is a map of where Russians buried anyone.
plates.location: Saratov and Simbirsk provinces (reports); Estonia and Belarus (corpus); Russian folktales (reading)
plates.tradition: Eastern Slavic and neighbouring folk belief

sections.heading: Outside the fence
paras: Dmitry Zelenin’s 1916 essays on those who died an ‘unnatural’ death collect local reports that such people were not always laid in the churchyard. Two are used here. At Orkino, in Saratov uezd, sudden deaths, drunkards, the drowned and suicides were buried far from the village, in the forest, in a ravine between two steep hills. In Silinskaya volost, Simbirsk guberniya, a ‘deaf forest ravine’ was held to be the proper grave for someone who had drunk himself to death, and burial in the cemetery was said to bring drought and crop failure.

Both are reports in someone else’s book, read here through excerpts. The Orkino report concerns half-Russified Mordvins. Zelenin’s own conclusions about two classes of the dead have been revised since, and the plate takes from him only what local people were reported to do and to fear.

sections.alt: A wide view along the edge of a mixed forest beside a railway line under open sky
sections.caption: A present-day forest edge beside a railway, Domodedovo, Moscow Oblast, 2022. Photograph: Artem Svetlov, CC0. It illustrates what an edge looks like. It is not a burial site and not evidence of any custom.

sections.heading: The forest on the road
paras: A 2025 comparative study of forest spirits by Mare Kõiva, Elena Boganeva and Ilya Butov remarks that in many rural cultures the forest is a place of hostile forces, or even of hell, and that the road to the realm of the dead is thought to run through it. The authors take that remark from an earlier author, Ivanov (1992), and present it as a common belief, not as their own finding.

The article’s sources are archives in Estonia and Belarus, with a small Russian-language sample from Estonia. It supports a widespread idea; it does not show how that idea was held in any Russian village.

sections.heading: A hut at the treeline
paras: Enrique Santos Marinas, reading the folktales Afanasyev published between 1855 and 1863, argues that the hut of Baba-Yaga stands at the forest edge or in a clearing because that position marks it as a threshold between two realms. On his reading the hut is a gateway to the Other World and its owner guards the passage.

This is a reading of narrative. A tale tells us what a teller expected an audience to recognise, which is not the same as what anyone did with a body. The plate keeps the hut as an image and does not use it as a record of belief.

sections.heading: Three kinds of evidence, three kinds of place
rows: Saratov and Simbirsk provinces; reports of local practice
That in these places some dead were buried in forest ravines and that cemetery burial was feared
Estonia and Belarus; archive texts about forest spirits
That a road to the dead through the forest is cited as a widespread belief
That the forest edge works as a threshold in the tales

sections.heading: What this plate does not say
items: It does not say that Russians generally buried anyone in forests. The one burial report from a Russian-speaking area is a single volost in Simbirsk province, and it is a report of belief about where a particular kind of dead person belonged.
It does not equate the forest spirit with the dead. The sources used here do not make that link, and the plate leaves it alone.
The Orkino report is Mordvin. Putting it on a plate about Russian death is a choice the plate makes openly and does not hide.

sections.heading: What would turn this plate into a study
items: Zelenin’s text itself, with page references for each local report and the correspondent named where he names one.
Regional ethnographic collections that record where drowned, suicides and unbaptised children were buried, village by village.
Archaeological or cemetery records of burials outside churchyards, kept apart from folklore.
Russian-language studies of the road to the other world, read in full.

plates.title: WATER, MARSH AND RIVER
plates.subtitle: Where the drowned were remembered, and where the swamp stood between worlds
plates.dek: In the sources read for this plate, water is the place of the drowned, and the swamp is a border. A calendar day remembered those who died by water; an essay reads swamps as a threshold. The plate keeps the dated custom and the interpretation apart.
plates.marginal: The calendar custom is reported by regions. The swamp essay spans many peoples and is not a Russian survey. The two do not prove each other.
plates.location: Vyatka, Smolensk and other provinces (Semik reports); Russia and neighbouring peoples (essay)
plates.tradition: Eastern Slavic folk custom; comparative mythology

sections.heading: A landscape in between
paras: Olga Lavrenova’s essay reads swamps in the mythopoetic picture of the peoples of Russia as a border landscape. A swamp joins water and land without being either, and in many of her examples it is also a place where souls go and where the living are in danger. Swamp spirits drag people down or lure them into the mire, and the kikimora of some accounts is a girl who drowned in a swamp.

The essay is a humanities argument built on secondary collections and has no stated way of choosing its examples. It ranges across Slavic, Finno-Ugric, Tungus, Turkic and other peoples, so a single detail cannot be assumed to be Russian. It tells us what a swamp can mean in these traditions. It does not tell us what any family did when someone drowned.

sections.alt: A wet bog with low pines and pools of standing water under a cloudy sky
sections.caption: A bog by Lake Lelikozero, Medvezhyegorsk district, Karelia, August 2014. Photograph: Evgenii Ievlev, CC BY-SA 4.0. A present-day landscape in the Russian North, shown to give the word ‘swamp’ a place. It is not tied to any rite.
sections.credit: Evgenii Ievlev / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

sections.heading: The drowned at Semik
paras: The Great Russian Encyclopedia’s online entry on Semik, the Thursday of the seventh week after Easter, describes it as a time to remember people who died without repentance or a funeral: the drowned, the hanged, victims of violence and the unidentified. In Vyatka the day was given to the drowned, and cemetery feasts there turned boisterous. In Smolensk province people avoided washing, rinsing or any work with water on that day so that no one in the family would drown. Wreaths and birches were thrown into rivers, and in some readings whether a wreath floated or sank signalled marriage or death.
The entry is anonymous and undated, and it names its regions without quoting the original records. The plate takes them as reports to be checked, not as a finished survey.

sections.heading: Pits for the unclaimed
paras: The same entry says that unidentified and unclaimed bodies were once placed in open communal pits, skudelnitsy, and buried together at Semik. Commemoration took place at cemeteries and at the sites of these ‘poor houses’. It adds that Catherine II banned burial in them in 1771.

That is a record of an institution, a place and a date. It is useful here because it shows the calendar custom attached to a physical arrangement for the dead who had no family to bury them. It says nothing about rivers.

sections.heading: Water in three kinds of source
rows: That some places remembered the drowned on a set day and avoided water on it
That swamps can be read as a border and a route for the dead in these traditions
That the afterlife of those who died by ‘unnatural’ death was placed on earth, in waters, bogs and forest thickets

sections.heading: What this plate does not say
items: It does not say that all Russians feared swimming or buried the drowned in a particular way. The sources used give isolated regional customs.
The Zelenin line is read from an excerpt, not from the book, and it is a general statement in a compilation; it is not tied to a village here.
Mermaids (rusalki) and the swamp spirits of folklore are not treated as the drowned themselves. That link belongs to a plate on the unquiet dead, which is not yet written.

sections.heading: What would turn this plate into a study
items: The original regional records behind the Semik entry, with collector, place and year.
Parish burial registers and police records for drownings, where archives allow it.
Studies of river and lake rites in the Russian North, read in full.
The full text of Zelenin’s chapters on water, with page references.

plates.title: ROADS, CROSSROADS AND BORDERS
plates.subtitle: Parting at the last crossroads, a reconstructed rite, and the crosses beside a modern highway
plates.dek: A crossroads is where a village ends, where relatives are seen off, and, in one scholar’s reconstruction, where some of the dead were once buried. A modern field count of roadside memorials gives the plate something firmer: 299 signs on three highways. The plate keeps the old reconstruction and the new count apart.
plates.marginal: The crossroads rite is a hypothesis built on fragments. The 299 signs are counted and photographed, but they mark road deaths of 1965–2019 in three Volga republics.
plates.location: Russian North (reconstruction); Chuvashia, Tatarstan and Mordovia (count)
plates.tradition: Eastern Slavic folk custom; contemporary roadside commemoration

sections.heading: Parting at the last crossroads
paras: N. A. Krinichnaya’s 1997 article on the crossroads, the Russian rosstan, records that it was the usual place to see travellers off and to wait for relatives returning after a long absence. The custom of parting at the village edge, at the nearest crossroads, she says, survived into her own time. Her material is mainly from the Russian North: Karelia, the Onega region, Vologda and Kostroma.
The article’s subject is fate, and parting is a side topic that it handles briefly. It gives no figures for how common the custom was.

sections.alt: A tall wooden Orthodox cross beside a snowy road junction, with a pine wood behind and a blue sign reading Reshma
sections.caption: A wooden cross at the turn to Reshma, Ivanovo Oblast, November 2011. Photograph: A-DIR, CC BY 3.0. The file does not say what the cross commemorates, and the plate does not guess.

sections.heading: A crossing as a burial ground
paras: Krinichnaya traces burial at crossroads to ancestor cults. In her reading a clan ancestor’s ashes were set on a pillar where roads met, a practice she links to a passage in the Primary Chronicle. She describes the later burial of people who died ‘unnaturally’, such as suicides, the drowned and unbaptised infants, at crossroads as a degenerate form of that older rite.

This is a reconstruction. It rests on fragmentary and often nineteenth-century records and on the idea of survivals, and the author’s own framing makes much of it hypothetical. The plate offers it as one scholar’s argument. It does not establish that any particular dead person was buried at any particular crossing.

sections.alt: A mounted warrior in mail stands before a tall inscribed stone on an open plain at dusk, with bones, a skull and ravens in the grass
sections.caption: *Knight at the Crossroads*, oil painting by Viktor Vasnetsov, 1878. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. The crossroads as an epic image: a stone with a warning, bones in the grass. It shows how the place was imagined in a painted bylina, not what was buried at any real crossing.
sections.credit: Viktor Vasnetsov / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

sections.heading: The roadside today
paras: M. G. Matlin’s geographical study recorded every roadside memorial sign on sections of three federal highways in the Middle Volga, photographing each, noting its coordinates and asking road workers and residents about it. He drove the routes repeatedly between 2013 and 2021 and documented 299 signs, whose dates of death run from 1965 to 2019.

He sorts them into two families. One imitates the cemetery with crosses, steles, obelisks, fenced plots and wreaths. The other does not, and uses flowerpots, gazebos, decorated trees and car parts. The boundary between them is loose. Placement differs by region: in Mordovia most signs stand on slopes, in Tatarstan in the roadside strip and in Chuvashia in or near woodland. He argues this differs from the European and North American habit of placing memorials right at the road edge.

sections.heading: What this plate does not say
items: It does not say that today’s roadside crosses descend from the crossroads rite. Neither source argues the link.

The count is of road-death signs on three routes in three republics. The author notes that the findings may not hold elsewhere, that density overstates what a driver sees, and that the idea of the road as a cemetery rests on drivers’ comments.
It does not describe the many other roadside cross traditions of Russia and its neighbours. The sources used here do not cover them.

sections.heading: What would turn this plate into a study
items: Regional ethnographic records of crossroads burial, with the place, year and collector named.
Studies of wayside and votive crosses at settlement edges, separate from road-death memorials.
A comparable count of roadside memorials in a Russian-majority region, to test whether the Middle Volga pattern holds.

plates.title: THE VANISHED VILLAGE
plates.subtitle: Flooded towns, uncounted graves and the villages that simply empty
plates.dek: Villages leave the map in two ways: the state floods them, or people leave. The Rybinsk Reservoir covered a town and hundreds of villages; the census records thousands of villages with no residents at all. The plate puts the two side by side and says what is and is not known about the dead who stayed.
plates.marginal: Figures for the flooded area come from a planning proposal. The claim about cemeteries under the water comes from a news feature seen only in an excerpt. Both are marked as such.
plates.location: Rybinsk Reservoir (Yaroslavl, Vologda and Tver oblasts); Russian Federation (census)

sections.heading: Water over the village
paras: E. A. Filatova’s 2026 planning article gives context figures for the Rybinsk and Uglich reservoirs on the Upper Volga: more than 300,000 hectares of fields, meadows and forest flooded, more than forty churches, three monasteries, about seven hundred villages and hamlets, and six towns, among them Mologa and Korcheva.
The article proposes lowering the reservoir to restore settlements, so it argues a case. In the part read, the figures carry no primary citation and there are no figures for graves or cemeteries.

sections.alt: A broad market square seen from above, with horse carts, trading rows, a two-storey stone building and a church with a bell tower in the distance
sections.caption: The market square of Mologa, early twentieth century. Photographer unknown; public domain as given on Commons. It shows the town before the reservoir. It does not show the flooding or the cemeteries.
sections.credit: Unknown photographer / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

sections.heading: Resettlement by decree
paras: I. Tsipileva’s article, written on Cherepovets district, states that resettlement followed a decree of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee and the Council of People’s Commissars of 1 August 1936, and that the residents of about seven hundred villages and hamlets were moved from the flood zone.
Only the opening of the article was seen, and its year of first publication is not shown. The decree is a dated document that a reader can look for. The article’s own focus is one district.

sections.alt: A small wooden chapel topped with a cross and a white bell-towered church on a bare rise, with a few figures between them
sections.caption: Mologa: a chapel and the Church of the Ascension, between 1901 and 1910 by Commons’ estimate. Photographer unknown; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (the file credits the Runivers project). A view of what was above ground before the water. It does not show the cemeteries, and it says nothing about what was done with them.
sections.credit: Unknown photographer / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

sections.heading: The cemeteries under the water
paras: A news feature published by RAPSI on 13 July 2026 says that the sanitary preparation of the reservoir bed was meant to include moving cemeteries, that in practice only some churchyards were moved in the 1930s and 1940s, and that many cemeteries of the Mologa area went under the water with their villages. It adds that estimates of the number resettled run from 100,000 to 130,000 and that historians dispute how they were counted.

This is unverified. The page could not be fetched, the lines were read in a search excerpt, and the excerpt cites no records. The plate treats it as a lead: the transfer of burials in the flood zone should be in archival files, and it is not in the sources read for this plate.

sections.heading: Two ways a village disappears
rows: Planning article; no primary citation seen
Report of the census report; 48% more than at the previous census

sections.heading: What this plate does not say
items: It does not give a number of graves or cemeteries lost. No source read here does, and the one claim about cemeteries is unverified.

It does not equate a flooded village with an uninhabited one. A flooded village was removed by decision; an uninhabited village in the census is a statistical status that says nothing about surviving buildings.
It does not retell the legends that grew around Mologa. They are not drawn from sources read here.

sections.heading: What would turn this plate into a study
items: Archival files on the transfer of burials from the flood zone, with the decree of 1 August 1936 and the orders that followed.
Parish records and cemetery registers for the flooded parishes, where they survive.
Oral-history collections from resettled families, with consent and attribution settled for private testimony.
The Rosstat census tables, to separate uninhabited villages by cause.
